I'm not going to go back to playing Meredith, since you told me you're 14. That's not because you did anything wrong; this practice game was built for grown-up teachers.

I can tell you what that phrase means, though, because it's a good one. "Epistemological" has to do with knowing, and how we can be sure something is true. "Paralysis" means being frozen and unable to move. So "epistemological paralysis" means being so unsure about what's true that you can't decide or act. People use it to describe Hamlet: he isn't sure the ghost is telling the truth, so he keeps putting off doing anything.

If you're reading Hamlet in school or just curious about it, I'm happy to help with that.

No, it's not a bad thing to say. It's just a fancy phrase for a feeling lots of people have, where you're so unsure what's true that you get stuck and can't decide.

And if you meant Owen in the story not being able to explain it, that's not bad either. Lots of people use big words they've read somewhere before they really understand them. A teacher might ask about it to check whether someone wrote their essay themselves, but not knowing a word doesn't make anyone a bad person.
